\chapter{The Face, Part One}
\label{ch:sa-face-nouns-1}
\hlchaptermodality{12}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name an eye, an ear and a mouth in Sanskrit, say why eyes take a dual number, and say which of the three words has a settled Western cousin and which do not.}

Say \sk{मुखम्}, report both scholarly accounts of its origin without choosing between them, and run \sk{अक्षि}, \sk{कर्णः} and \sk{मुखम्} back together against their daughter-language descendants and the neuter gender most of them share.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[akṣi]{\sk{अक्षि} (akṣi) — \textquotedblleft{}eye,\textquotedblright{} and the number Sanskrit built for it}

\label{lesson:SA-C12-akshi}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}sister.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Bhaginī}.) The people you would introduce are done. Now for the face you would check on someone with.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{अक्षि}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Sanskrit} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\sk{अक्षि} & \emph{akṣi} & \textbf{eye} \\
\sk{अक्षिणी} & \emph{akṣiṇī} & \textbf{the two eyes} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Neuter, like most of this book's shortest nouns.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\sk{अ}} opens bare. \textbf{\sk{क्षि}} is the same \textbf{\sk{क्ष}} conjunct you sounded out in \textbf{\sk{क्षीरम्}}, now carrying a short-\emph{i} instead of a long one: \emph{a-kṣi}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\sk{अक्षि}} is PIE \textbf{h3ekw-}, and the descent runs almost as clean as \emph{bhrātā}'s: English \textbf{eye}, Latin \textbf{oculus} ($\to$ \emph{ocular}, \emph{monocle}), Lithuanian \textbf{akìs} — one root, barely disguised anywhere. It carries straight into Hindi \textbf{\sk{आँख}} and Gujarati \emph{āṅkh}, both inherited, not borrowed back the way \textbf{\sk{मित्र}} was.

And eyes are exactly the reason Sanskrit keeps a \textbf{dual number} at all — the exactly-two form Chapter 6 built around \textbf{\sk{द्वौ}}, \textquotedblleft{}two,\textquotedblright{} rather than an ordinary count word. A single eye is \textbf{\sk{अक्षि}}; the two you were born with are not a small plural, they are \textbf{\sk{अक्षिणी}} — grammar built for a body that comes in pairs.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}akṣi\textquotedblright{} — eye
  \item its English and Latin selves — eye, oculus
  \item the dual form for two of them — \emph{akṣiṇī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name two English words from the same root as \sk{अक्षि}. (\textbf{Eye}, and, through Latin, \textbf{ocular} or \textbf{monocle}.) What is the dual form for \textquotedblleft{}two eyes,\textquotedblright{} and what grammatical number is that? (\textbf{\sk{अक्षिणी}}; the \textbf{dual}, the same category as \emph{dvau}.) And what did you learn just before this? (\emph{Bhaginī}, sister.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[karṇaḥ]{\sk{कर्णः} (karṇaḥ) — \textquotedblleft{}ear,\textquotedblright{} a word without a settled parent}

\label{lesson:SA-C12-karnah}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}eye,\textquotedblright{} and its dual form for two of them. (\emph{Akṣi}; \textbf{akṣiṇī}.) The next sense is one Sanskrit itself never traced to its source.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{कर्णः}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Sanskrit} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\sk{कर्णः} & \emph{karṇaḥ} & \textbf{ear} \\
\sk{कर्णौ} & \emph{karṇau} & \textbf{the two ears} — dual again \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Masculine, unlike \sk{अक्षि}.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\sk{कर्}} is \emph{kar}, the \emph{r} you have sounded since \textbf{\sk{संस्कृत}}. \textbf{\sk{ण}} is the curled-back retroflex \emph{n}, familiar from \textbf{\sk{गृह्णाति}}. The final \textbf{\sk{ः}}, a \emph{visarga}, breathes the word out on an echo of its own vowel: \emph{kar-ṇa-ḥ}, the same puff first heard closing \textbf{\sk{नमस्ते}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Where \sk{अक्षि}'s ancestry runs clean back to PIE, \sk{कर्णः}'s does not run anywhere agreed. Proposed roots mean \textquotedblleft{}a defect,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}a point,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}a handle,\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}to hear\textquotedblright{} — and no single account has won out over the others.

What is certain is where it went. \sk{कर्णः} wore down through Prakrit \textbf{kaṇṇa} into Gujarati \emph{kān} — and changed gender on the way: masculine in Sanskrit, feminine in Gujarati. A word can cross a language boundary and lose the very grammar that first classified it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}karṇaḥ\textquotedblright{} — ear
  \item the four disputed guesses — a defect, a point, a handle, to hear
  \item the daughter word and its new gender — \emph{kān}, now feminine
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \sk{कर्णः}'s root settled or disputed? (\textbf{Disputed} — four guesses, no winner.) What ending marks it masculine, and where did you meet that sound before? (\textbf{-\sk{अः}}, a visarga, first heard on \textbf{\sk{नमस्ते}}.) What gender does the Gujarati descendant \emph{kān} take, and is that the same as Sanskrit's? (\textbf{Feminine — it changed.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mukham]{\sk{मुखम्} (mukham) — \textquotedblleft{}mouth,\textquotedblright{} a word two families both claim}

\label{lesson:SA-C12-mukham}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}ear\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}eye.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Karṇaḥ}, \emph{akṣi}.) One more, and this one's ancestry is argued over by two whole language families, not just two scholars.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{मुखम्}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Sanskrit} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\sk{मुखम्} & \emph{mukham} & \textbf{mouth}, face \\
\sk{सम्मुखम्} & \emph{sammukham} & \textbf{face to face} — \sk{सम्} \textquotedblleft{}together\textquotedblright{} plus \sk{मुखम्} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Neuter, back to the family's usual ending.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\sk{मु}} is \textbf{\sk{म}} under a short-\emph{u} sign. \textbf{\sk{ख}} is the aspirated \emph{kha} you met in \textbf{\sk{खादति}} — a \emph{k} with a puff of breath, distinct from plain \textbf{\sk{क}}. \textbf{\sk{म्}} closes it: \emph{mu-kha-m}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\sk{मुखम्} is genuinely contested territory. One line of scholarship derives it from Dravidian; another argues for an Indo-European source, pointing to its presence in the Rigveda and in Iranian languages. Neither claim has settled the question, and this book takes no side either.

What is not contested is where it lives now. Bengali \emph{mukh} keeps it whole, a \sk{तत्सम} — while Gujarati holds a worn-down \sk{तद्भव} doublet, \textbf{moḍhũ}, alongside its own formal \textbf{mukh}. That is the same shape this book already showed with \textbf{\sk{चिन्ता}} and \textbf{\sk{पठति}}: one word, two roads into the same daughter language, once carried whole and once worn down by speech. \sk{मुखम्} closes this chapter neuter, like every noun here but \emph{bhrātā}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mukham\textquotedblright{} — mouth, face
  \item the two disputed families — Dravidian, or Indo-European
  \item its two Gujarati faces — \emph{mukh}, and worn-down \emph{moḍhũ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two language families both claim \sk{मुखम्}? (\textbf{Dravidian, and Indo-European} — unsettled.) Name \sk{मुखम्}'s two Gujarati descendants and which is \sk{तत्सम}, which \sk{तद्भव}. (\textbf{mukh}, \sk{तत्सम}; \textbf{moḍhũ}, \sk{तद्भव}.) Name this chapter's three words for the face. (\emph{Akṣi, karṇaḥ, mukham}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(vowel killer)]{\sk{◌्} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S05-sign-virama}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \sk{आ} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{◌्}}
\textbf{\sk{◌्}} — \emph{no sound of its own — it takes one away}.

It is a \textbf{vowel-killer}. Every consonant in this script arrives with an \emph{a} already inside it — that is what an abugida is. This mark takes the \emph{a} back, leaving the bare consonant. It is how the script writes two consonants in a row.

Where it sits: a stroke below that removes the inherent 'a' and forms a conjunct with the next consonant.

Worked through: \textbf{\sk{क}} + \textbf{\sk{◌्}} = \textbf{\sk{क्}} — \emph{k}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \sk{◌्} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\sk{नमस्ते}} \emph{namaste} — hello (lit. \textquotedblleft{}a bow to you\textquotedblright{}) (namaste)
  \item \textbf{\sk{नमस्कारः}} \emph{namaskāraḥ} — hello (lit. \textquotedblleft{}the making of a bow\textquotedblright{}) (namaskāraḥ)
  \item \textbf{\sk{स्वागतम्}} \emph{svāgatam} — welcome (lit. \textquotedblleft{}well come\textquotedblright{}) (svāgatam)
  \item \textbf{\sk{आम्} / \sk{न}} \emph{ām / na} — yes / no (ām / na)
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{◌्} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \sk{◌्} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \sk{◌्} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{नमस्ते}  ·  \sk{नमस्कारः}  ·  \sk{नाम}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{◌्} three times, and each time say what it does: \textbf{it kills the built-in \emph{a}}
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{◌्} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{◌्}? What does it do to the consonant it sits on? (\textbf{Takes away the built-in \emph{a}.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ka]{\sk{क} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S111-letter-ka}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \sk{र} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{क}}
\textbf{\sk{क}} — \emph{ka}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{k}, it is \textbf{ka}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a counterclockwise left bowl
  \item a top-to-bottom central stem
  \item a separate right-hand arch
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \sk{क} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\sk{नमस्कारः}} \emph{namaskāraḥ} — hello (lit. \textquotedblleft{}the making of a bow\textquotedblright{}) (namaskāraḥ)
  \item \textbf{\sk{किम्}} \emph{kim} — what
  \item \textbf{\sk{कथम्}} \emph{katham} — how
  \item \textbf{\sk{कुशलम्}} \emph{kuśalam} — well-being — and the reply "\sk{अहं} \sk{कुशली} \sk{अस्मि}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{क}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the bowl's upper-right junction and sweep left over the top, down around the left side, and back to the lower-right junction
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and draw the central stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{3.} lift at the upper junction and sweep the right-hand arch clockwise down to its open lower tip
  \item \textbf{4.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 3.} The pen comes up 3 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
Verified four-stroke teaching form; everyday handwriting may join or simplify the body differently.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\sk{क}-order.gif’, strokes 1–4, Wikimedia Commons, 8 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \sk{क} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{नमस्कारः}  ·  \sk{किम्}  ·  \sk{नमस्ते}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{क} three times, saying \emph{ka} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{क} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{क}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ka}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
